Entry **#111** in Andrew Gelman's [Handy Statistical Lexicon](https://statmodeling.stat.columbia.edu/2009/05/24/handy_statistic/). Original discussion: [source post](https://statmodeling.stat.columbia.edu/2014/12/12/saying-things-place/).

## What it is

A number or a story taken by itself means little. "Crime rose 8% this year" could be alarming or routine depending on how much the rate usually moves from year to year. "The treatment improved scores by 3 points" depends on the scale, the spread and what other interventions achieve. A statistic exists in context: its history, its natural variability and its comparison points.

## Why it matters

Journalism and research communication often report changes without the baseline needed to interpret them. Readers can't tell a meaningful shift from ordinary fluctuation, so every uptick becomes a trend and every downturn a crisis. Giving context, such as the typical year-to-year change, the long-run range or a comparable effect, turns a factoid into information.

## How it works

Judge a change $\Delta$ relative to the distribution of changes you would expect anyway. With historical year-to-year changes $\Delta_1, \dots, \Delta_T$, the percentile of the new $\Delta$ among them, or $\Delta / \mathrm{sd}(\Delta_t)$, tells you whether it is unusual. The same $\Delta$ is huge in a stable series and trivial in a volatile one.

## Simulated example

Every headline reports the same "+8% this year." Choose how volatile the underlying series is and see what that 8% actually means.

```{ojs}
import {rng, range, sd, fmt, pct} from "../js/stats.js"
```

```{ojs}
viewof volatility = Inputs.range([1, 20], {value: 3, step: 0.5, label: "Typical year-to-year change (%)"})
viewof headline = Inputs.range([0, 30], {value: 8, step: 0.5, label: "This year's reported change (%)"})
viewof seed = Inputs.range([1, 500], {value: 111, step: 1, label: "Random seed"})
```

```{ojs}
history = {
  const r = rng(seed);
  return range(40).map(t => ({year: 1985 + t, change: r.normal(0, volatility)}));
}
```

```{ojs}
Plot.plot({
  height: 280,
  x: {label: "Year", tickFormat: "d"},
  y: {label: "Year-to-year change (%)", grid: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleX(history, {x: "year", y: "change", stroke: "#999", strokeWidth: 4}),
    Plot.ruleX([{year: 2025, change: headline}], {x: "year", y: "change", stroke: "#d6604d", strokeWidth: 6}),
    Plot.text([{year: 2025, change: headline}], {x: "year", y: "change", text: () => "this year", dy: -10, fill: "#d6604d"}),
    Plot.ruleY([0])
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const larger = history.filter(d => Math.abs(d.change) >= headline).length;
  return html`<div class="sim-readout">${md`In the past 40 years, **${larger}** years had a change at least as large as this year's ${headline}%. This year is **${fmt(headline / sd(history.map(d => d.change)), 1)} sd** from zero. ${larger > 6 ? "In context, it's routine." : "In context, it really is unusual."} Same headline, different stories.`}</div>`;
}
```

## Key takeaways

::: takeaways
- A statistic means something only against its context: history, variability and comparisons.
- Report how unusual a change is, not just its size.
- When you see a bare number, ask what it should be compared with.
:::
